title: Liver Ketogenesis

reactions.name: Thiolase condensation
reactions.notes: 2 Acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA + CoA. Reversible reaction; in beta-oxidation the same enzyme runs in the thiolytic cleavage direction. In ketogenesis, the condensation direction is driven forward by the high acetyl-CoA concentration that accumulates when TCA flux is limited by low OAA.

reactions.name: HMG-CoA synthesis
reactions.notes: Acetoacetyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA + H2O → HMG-CoA + CoA. This is the rate-limiting and regulated step of ketogenesis. The mitochondrial isoform (HMGCS2) is distinct from the cytosolic isoform (HMGCS1) involved in cholesterol synthesis. HMGCS2 is inhibited by succinyl-CoA (competitive with acetoacetyl-CoA), linking TCA activity to ketogenic flux: when the TCA runs (succinyl-CoA present), ketogenesis is braked. HMGCS2 gene expression is induced by fasting via PPAR-alpha and FGF21 signalling and repressed by insulin.

reactions.name: HMG-CoA cleavage
reactions.notes: HMG-CoA → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA. Irreversible. Acetoacetate is the primary ketone body exported from the mitochondrion. Note that one acetyl-CoA is regenerated, which can enter the TCA or condense with another acetyl-CoA in the next cycle.

reactions.name: Acetoacetate reduction to beta-hydroxybutyrate
reactions.notes: Acetoacetate + NADH + H+ → beta-hydroxybutyrate + NAD+. Reversible reaction (direction depends on NADH/NAD+ ratio). During active beta-oxidation, NADH is high, favouring beta-hydroxybutyrate formation. The ratio of beta-OHB to acetoacetate in plasma reflects mitochondrial NADH/NAD+, used clinically as an indicator of redox state. Beta-OHB is the predominant circulating ketone (typically 2-3 x more than acetoacetate). A small fraction of acetoacetate undergoes spontaneous non-enzymatic decarboxylation to acetone + CO2 (the smell on the breath of ketotic patients).

regulationRules.mechanism: Succinyl-CoA competitively inhibits HMGCS2 at the acetoacetyl-CoA binding site. When the TCA cycle is running at full speed (e.g., fed state), succinyl-CoA is present and ketogenesis is braked. When OAA is depleted by gluconeogenesis (deep fasting), TCA flux falls, succinyl-CoA drops, and HMGCS2 is relieved.

Prolonged fasting raises plasma NEFA, which activate PPAR-alpha in hepatocytes. PPAR-alpha induces HMGCS2 gene transcription (and also the enzymes of beta-oxidation and fatty acid uptake). This transcriptional upregulation increases ketogenic capacity over hours to days of fasting. FGF21 (a fasting-induced hepatokine) potentiates PPAR-alpha signalling.

Insulin represses HMGCS2 gene expression via Akt-mediated phosphorylation and nuclear exclusion of FOXA2, a transcription factor required for HMGCS2 induction. Insulin also suppresses adipose lipolysis, reducing NEFA supply to the liver and thus limiting the acetyl-CoA input to ketogenesis.

OAA is a substrate for both citrate synthase (TCA) and PEPCK (gluconeogenesis). In deep fasting, gluconeogenesis draws heavily on OAA (via PEPCK), and the TCA slows because it cannot receive acetyl-CoA without OAA. Acetyl-CoA accumulates, driving the thiolase condensation forward and increasing HMG-CoA synthesis. This is the key metabolic logic: gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis rise together in prolonged fasting because they share the OAA depletion signal.

Beta-oxidation generates NADH in the mitochondrial matrix. The high NADH/NAD+ ratio (also seen in alcoholism) drives BHBD in the direction of beta-hydroxybutyrate formation, so plasma beta-OHB rises disproportionately relative to acetoacetate. The beta-OHB/acetoacetate ratio is used clinically as a proxy for the mitochondrial NADH/NAD+ ratio.

teachingSequence: During prolonged fasting, glucagon-stimulated lipolysis delivers large amounts of NEFA to the liver. Beta-oxidation runs at high rate, generating acetyl-CoA faster than the TCA cycle can consume it.
The TCA cycle is limited because OAA is drawn away by active gluconeogenesis (PEPCK). Without OAA, acetyl-CoA cannot condense into citrate at citrate synthase.

Excess acetyl-CoA is diverted to the ketogenic pathway. Mitochondrial thiolase condenses two acetyl-CoA to acetoacetyl-CoA, and the rate-limiting enzyme HMGCS2 adds another acetyl-CoA to form HMG-CoA.

HMGCS2 is the gatekeeper: it is inhibited by succinyl-CoA (fed state, TCA running) and induced transcriptionally by PPAR-alpha during prolonged fasting. Succinyl-CoA falls when the TCA slows, relieving HMGCS2 inhibition.
HMG-CoA lyase cleaves HMG-CoA to acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA. The regenerated acetyl-CoA can re-enter the cycle, amplifying ketone output.

Beta-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase reduces acetoacetate to beta-hydroxybutyrate, driven by the high NADH generated by beta-oxidation. Beta-OHB (the predominant circulating ketone body) is exported to the bloodstream.

In peripheral tissues (heart, skeletal muscle, renal cortex, and after adaptation, the brain), beta-OHB and acetoacetate are converted back to acetyl-CoA via succinyl-CoA: 3-ketoacid CoA transferase (OXCT1) and thiolase, providing a highly efficient fuel that the liver itself cannot oxidise (it lacks OXCT1).
clinicalLinks: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): in type 1 diabetes, absolute insulin deficiency removes all three brakes on ketogenesis (lipolysis uninhibited, HMGCS2 unrepressed, beta-oxidation unrestricted). Plasma ketone bodies rise to 10-25 mM (normal: <0.5 mM), causing severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3). Ketones are acids; their buffering consumes bicarbonate. Emergency treatment: insulin + IV fluids + potassium.

Starvation ketosis: after 3-5 days of total fasting, plasma ketones reach 5-7 mM. The brain adapts to use beta-OHB as its primary fuel, sparing glucose and thereby reducing muscle proteolysis. This is a physiological, compensated acidosis, distinct from DKA in its slower onset and lower magnitude.

Therapeutic ketosis: very-low-carbohydrate (ketogenic) diets raise plasma ketones to 1-3 mM. Used as adjunct therapy in drug-resistant epilepsy (since the 1920s) and investigated in metabolic syndrome and certain cancers.

Alcoholic ketoacidosis: excess ethanol oxidation generates massive NADH, inhibiting gluconeogenesis and driving the BHBD reaction toward beta-OHB. Presents with elevated anion-gap acidosis, low or normal glucose, and a high beta-OHB/acetoacetate ratio.

HMGCL deficiency: rare autosomal recessive disorder. Cannot complete ketogenesis. Presents in neonates or infancy with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, and metabolic acidosis triggered by fasting. Organic acid analysis shows elevated 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA intermediates.

MCAD deficiency (indirect link): impaired beta-oxidation reduces acetyl-CoA supply to ketogenesis. During illness, these patients are at risk of hypoketotic hypoglycaemia because they cannot mount a ketogenic response to fasting.
